title: The Balmer Absorber Strength Problem of Little Red Dots
abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) commonly show Balmer absorption features. Some observed LRD spectra have weaker absorption in H$α$ than in H$β$, in apparent contradiction to atomic physics according to standard attenuation models. This tension is naturally resolved when one considers emission from the absorbing medium itself, which is ignored in the standard model: when the Balmer absorption is optically thick, a non-negligible source function could fill in the H$α$ absorption trough and reduce its observed absorption equivalent width (EW). With proof-of-concept photoionization models we show that the source function of H$α$ could be systematically stronger than that of H$β$. This is due to radiative trapping preferentially populating the $n=3$ level of neutral hydrogen, which operates efficiently when the medium is optically thick to H$α$ but not very optically thick to Paschen-$α$. Such line-dependent source functions could lead to significant corrections to the expected EW and selectively weaken H$α$ absorption, consistent with observations. Quantitatively, this depends on the distance of the absorbing medium and its internal structure, providing a new diagnostic of the environment around LRDs. Future modeling of the absorbers may also potentially open a new avenue for estimating the mass of the central engine.

title: Resolving the extended interstellar medium of infrared galaxies I. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emission
abstract: We investigate spatial variations in polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) properties and photoelectric heating efficiency in 67 nearby luminous infrared galaxies from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Using mid-infrared spectroscopy from Spitzer and far-infrared cooling-line maps from Herschel, we extract spectra in concentric annuli and matched aperture grids out to about 14 kpc. PAH features are measured with the CAFE spectral decomposition tool. We trace photoelectric heating efficiency by combining PAH emission with cooling lines after isolating the neutral-gas contribution. In starburst galaxies, the PAH 11.3/7.7 ratio rises out to about 5 kpc while 6.2/7.7 remains nearly constant, indicating predominantly large, neutral PAHs. Between 5 and 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 continues to rise while inferred PAH sizes decrease. Beyond 8 kpc, 11.3/7.7 falls and 6.2/7.7 rises, indicating smaller, more ionized PAHs. These trends are consistent with PAH photodestruction near the central starburst. Strong active galactic nucleus (AGN) systems show more neutral PAHs and harder radiation fields in their nuclear and inner regions. Beyond about 5 kpc, PAHs become more ionized and approach the starburst locus as the radiation field weakens. Strong AGNs influence average PAH charge states at 6-14 kpc as effectively as moderate AGNs at 1-6 kpc. Photoelectric heating efficiency increases with radius in both starburst and AGN-hosting galaxies as the radiation field weakens. In starbursts, higher efficiency is associated with more neutral PAHs, while AGN-dominated systems show the opposite relation. These results provide quantitative, spatially resolved constraints on the extent of AGN effects on dust properties in a population of luminous infrared galaxies.
title_ja: 赤外線銀河の拡張星間媒質の解明 I. 多環芳香族炭化水素の放射

title: Resolving the extended interstellar medium of infrared galaxies II. Fine-structure line emission
abstract: We investigate how star formation and active galactic nuclei (AGNs) shape the ionized and neutral interstellar medium in 67 nearby luminous and ultraluminous infrared galaxies from the Great Observatories All-sky LIRG Survey (GOALS). Combining mid-infrared (MIR) spectral mapping from the Spitzer Infrared Spectrograph with far-infrared (FIR) spectroscopy from the Herschel Photodetector Array Camera and Spectrometer, we measure fine-structure emission lines in aperture grids extending to projected galactocentric distances of about 14 kpc. We compare the measurements with CLOUDY photoionization models to constrain the ionization parameter, hydrogen density, stellar age, and metallicity. In starburst-dominated galaxies, the combined MIR+FIR fits yield a decreasing ionization parameter with radius, approximately constant hydrogen densities, uniformly young stellar populations, and flat metallicity profiles. MIR-only fits instead yield an increasing ionization parameter with radius, highlighting the importance of FIR diagnostics, particularly the [C II] emission associated with photodissociation regions, in constraining the multiphase gas. In the strongest AGN-dominated system, the nucleus and inner extended regions show elevated [Ne III]/[Ne II] and suppressed [C II]/[O I] ratios, while the outermost regions, at projected distances of about 6 kpc and beyond, show values typical of star-forming regions. This suggests that the AGN may affect gas excitation out to about 5 kpc. Our results demonstrate the importance of combining MIR and FIR diagnostics to recover radial trends that can be hidden in galaxy-integrated measurements. Together with Paper I, they provide a benchmark for spatially resolved studies of gas and dust in starbursts and AGN-hosting galaxies.

title: Large fluctuations and cusp-core transformation in dwarf galaxies
abstract: Dwarf galaxies are abundant and dark matter dominated, rendering them particularly relevant for testing a cosmological model dominated by a dark sector. Whether their density profiles agree with $Λ$CDM expectations has long been a point of contention, dubbed the cusp/core problem. While numerical simulations have suggested that the erasure of central dark matter cusps may arise from potential fluctuations in feedback-driven gas, whether the required fluctuation levels are achieved in actual galaxies has remained uncertain. By measuring the power spectra of neutral gas density contrasts in a sample of gas-rich dwarf galaxies, we show that the observed fluctuations match theoretical expectations when their impact is derived from a stochastic dynamical model. Specifically, the relaxation times for core formation at the observationally estimated radii are generally on the order of a Hubble time or less. Core sizes are therefore consistent with conservative estimates assuming their generation through steady fluctuations acting over cosmic history. The relaxation time increases with halo mass, suggesting that core formation via this mechanism becomes less efficient in more massive systems.

title: The clumpy fraction of galaxies at $z=1-9$ with JADES: evidence for a mass-dependent transition in clump origin
abstract: We measure the fraction of clumpy galaxies ($f_{\rm clumpy}$) over the redshift range $z=1-9$ and stellar masses $\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot}) \geq 8$ using JWST/NIRCam imaging from JADES. We define clumps as compact off-centre surface-brightness peaks with characteristic sizes of a few hundred parsecs, and develop a dendrogram-based clump-finding method with astrodendro to identify them directly in rest-frame UV, blue, and optical images. Clump-detection completeness is quantified through injection-recovery simulations, which we use to define ($M_\star$, $z$)-dependent 50 per cent completeness-limited $f_{\rm clumpy}$, alongside a probability-weighted completeness-corrected statistic for comparison. For the full sample, the blue and optical $f_{\rm clumpy}$ reach $\approx55$ per cent at $z\approx1-2$ and decline to $\lesssim5$ per cent by $z\approx8-9$, while the UV fraction remains higher at $\approx12$ per cent. At $z\approx1-2$, $f_{\rm clumpy}$ increases strongly with stellar mass, from $\approx35$ per cent in the lowest-mass bin to $\approx85$ per cent at $\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})\geq10$. Most clumpy galaxies host only one or two robustly detected off-centre clumps, while higher-multiplicity systems occur preferentially in massive, strongly star-forming galaxies at low to intermediate redshift. Comparison with major merger rates suggests that mergers could account for a substantial fraction of low-mass ($\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})<8.5$), high-redshift clumpy galaxies, while the observed fractions in more massive systems ($\log_{10}(M_\star/{\rm M_\odot})>9$) require an additional in situ clump-formation channel. Our results are consistent with a transition from merger-dominated clumpy morphologies at early times and low stellar masses to an increasing contribution from in situ clump-formation channels, such as disc instabilities, in more massive systems.

title: KMOS Spectroscopic Follow-up of 16 Star Cluster Candidates of the Sagittarius Dwarf Galaxy
abstract: The Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf spheroidal galaxy hosts several known globular clusters and numerous additional cluster candidates identified toward its crowded central regions. Establishing the nature of these candidates is difficult because apparent spatial and astrometric structure can arise from the underlying Sgr population. We investigate sixteen Minni stellar-cluster candidates with KMOS spectroscopy to determine whether the observed stars are compatible with Sgr and whether any candidate field shows evidence for a distinct stellar system. We analyse H-band KMOS spectra of 341 targets from the VVVX-GalCen Spectroscopic Survey, deriving radial velocities (RVs) and empirical metallicities. We compare these with an independent Sgr spectroscopic sample and use VVVX photometry and Gaia DR3 astrometry to test for localized stellar excesses relative to local control fields. Of the 341 KMOS targets, 256 (75%) have RVs within the adopted Sgr interval, and their metallicities broadly overlap the Sgr comparison population. No field shows statistically compelling kinematic evidence for a distinct system after accounting for the multiple candidates examined. Minni 329 shows the strongest spatial excess, but this is not significant after multiple-testing correction and is not accompanied by significant central concentration. The KMOS targets predominantly trace the Sgr population, but Sgr compatibility alone does not confirm the individual candidates as distinct stellar clusters. None of the sixteen fields can be confirmed as a separate stellar system with the present data, although this does not establish that the original candidates are spurious. Deeper imaging and larger spectroscopic samples are required to determine their physical nature.

title: Coevolution of Dust Growth and Gravitational Instability in Massive Protostellar Disks
abstract: Massive protostellar disks are expected to sustain high accretion rates through gravitational instability, while dust growth may modify their opacity, cooling efficiency, and stability. Conversely, the time-dependent and nonaxisymmetric structures produced by gravitational instability may regulate the local conditions for dust growth. However, the coupled evolution of dust growth and gravitational instability in massive protostellar disks has not yet been explored self-consistently. We present two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations that follow gas dynamics, dust growth, and opacity-dependent radiative cooling in a massive protostellar disk. We find that dust grains rapidly grow to millimeter-centimeter sizes shortly after disk formation, substantially reducing the infrared opacity. The enhanced cooling promotes disk fragmentation and produces more frequent accretion-driven luminosity outbursts than in a model without dust growth, with durations and peak luminosities comparable to those observed in massive protostars. Dust growth is broadly regulated by the fragmentation-limited size in dense disk regions, whereas newly formed outer disk regions and low-density regions deviate from this limit because of finite collision timescales and dust transport. These results suggest that dust growth may facilitate episodic accretion and fragmentation, while gravitationally unstable disk structures in turn regulate the dust growth process.

title: Pulsar J1909+0749 and Supernova Remnant G42.1-0.2: A case of a pulsar that has exited the shell of its associated supernova remnant
abstract: (Abridged) The ATNF pulsar catalogue features only 63 pulsars that are possibly associated with a supernova remnant (SNR). Even rarer is the scenario in which the pulsar has escaped the physical extent of its corresponding SNR. We aim to identify the serendipitously discovered shell-type object G42.1-0.2 as a SNR. The known pulsar (PSR) J1909+0749 lies well outside the shell of SNR G42.1-0.2, but it has a cometary tail pointing towards the centre of the SNR; we propose that the SNR and the pulsar originated from the same supernova explosion. By measuring the flux densities of the shell G42.1-0.2 from ${\sim}$200 MHz to ${\sim}$6 GHz, we establish the nonthermal nature of its emission. With the characteristic age of the pulsar, its distance from the Sun estimated from the dispersion measure (DM), and the angular separation between the pulsar and the centre of the shell, we infer the evolutionary state of the SNR and the transverse velocity of the pulsar. Using proper motion measurements, we compare the SNR-pulsar direction with the velocity of the pulsar. The radio spectral index of the shell is $-0.36 \pm 0.08$, confirming that the emission is primarily nonthermal synchrotron. The proper motion measurements are not well constrained, but the amplitude and the direction are consistent with the interpretation that the SNR and the pulsar are associated. If the characteristic age and the DM-based distance represent the true age and the true distance of the pulsar and the SNR, then the standard evolution equations suggest that the SNR must still be in the Sedov-Taylor phase, evolving in a medium with a density of about 1.5 cm$^{-3}$. In addition, as a result of the PSR-SNR association, the transverse velocity of the pulsar PSR J1909+0749 is estimated to be ${\sim}1460~\mathrm{km\,s}^{-1}$, ranking it among the highest transverse velocities observed for pulsars in the Milky Way.

title: Kinematically isolating intracluster light in AS1063: a distinct stellar population tracing the dark matter core
abstract: We present a technique using integral-field spectroscopy to kinematically isolate intracluster light (ICL) from the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG), enabling insights into their contrasting stellar populations and the inner dark matter halo profile. Applying this technique to MUSE data of Abell S1063, we find that both components are old (~9 Gyr), but the ICL is more metal-poor than the BCG, implying distinct progenitor pathways. Within 100 kpc, the ICL comprises 55 per cent of the BCG+ICL stellar mass - substantially more than inferred from photometric decompositions. The BCG and ICL possess distinct velocity distributions, which remain nearly constant with radius, with an ICL velocity dispersion more than twice that of the BCG, and a line-of-sight velocity offset of 86 +- 18 km/s. Two-dimensional Sérsic fits yield an ICL centroid offset of 5.2 +- 1.5 kpc from the BCG. These phase-space offsets are indicative of the BCG oscillating in a broad potential minimum. Furthermore, the ICL surface-brightness profile matches that of strong-lensing estimates assuming a cored halo. Simulations indicate that the inner halo profile varies systematically for different dark matter models. Applied to larger samples, our method therefore offers a complementary route to testing the nature of dark matter, while simultaneously revealing the stellar origins of the ICL.

title: Phakoseismology: Asteroseismology of gravitationally microlensed stars
abstract: Asteroseismology relies on disk-integrated photometry or radial velocities, in which geometric cancellation suppresses modes of high spherical degree ($l\geq4$). Observations are thus limited to deeply penetrating, low-degree modes, leaving the outer envelope inaccessible. We investigate whether a high-magnification microlensing event can temporarily lift this limitation by differentially magnifying the surface of an oscillating source star. We modelled the visibility of solar-like oscillations during microlensing, weighting the surface by limb darkening and the local magnification. We computed multiplet visibilities and the power distribution among azimuthal components, and built a likelihood model for recovering the 3D spin-axis orientation from resolved rotational multiplets. When the lens-source separation becomes comparable to the source's angular radius, the magnification gradient acts as a transient spatial filter that breaks the symmetry of disk integration, raising high-degree mode visibilities by up to three orders of magnitude. The same non-axisymmetric weighting makes the relative power of azimuthal components depend on both the inclination and sky-projected azimuth of the spin axis, imprinting the full spin orientation onto the power spectrum. With $5\%$ relative-power uncertainties, we recover the orientation to $σ_i=2.9^\circ$ and $σ_γ=11.5^\circ$. Microlensing thus does more than amplify distant stars: its magnification pattern enables spatially selective asteroseismology. The effect is strongest for rare close encounters and unlikely to support large samples, and the newly visible high-degree modes will overlap with rotationally split and mixed modes, complicating mode identification. Nevertheless, individual high-quality events may open a window on envelope physics and spin geometries for stars in the Galactic bulge and beyond.

title: Understanding the formation of alpha-Fe bimodality in the Milky Way using constrained cosmological simulations of the Local Group
abstract: We use a novel suite of constrained cosmological simulations of the Local Group to investigate the formation of alpha--Fe bimodalities in stellar discs of Milky Way analogues. In agreement with past studies using the Auriga model, we show that in our simulations the high-alpha sequence forms in a merger-induced starburst, which further quenches star formation, allowing the new stellar populations to form at low [alpha/Fe]. Producing a bimodality that is prominent at large radii, with a significant [alpha/Fe] gap and overlapping metallicity as in the Milky Way, requires the quenching of star formation across all radii where the bimodality is observed. The quenching can be achieved either with a galaxy-wide starburst, or with a retrograde merger reducing angular momentum in the outer disc and allowing more efficient dilution by the metal-poor gas in the circumgalactic medium (CGM). We show that mergers can also tilt the disc, changing the direction of galactic outflows and enriching a larger volume of the CGM with galactic metals, leading to low [alpha/Fe] scatter in the subsequently formed low-alpha sequence. We argue that the slopes in [alpha/Fe] of the two alpha sequences are crucial in narrowing down the mechanism that leads to their formation. We additionally uncover an indirect role that mergers play in enhancing the accretion of metal-poor gas onto galaxies. The smoothly accreted gas can dominate the gas content in the CGM and aid in the formation of distinct chemical sequences, especially at the low-metallicity end.

title: VVV CL001: A strong candidate for the most ancient star cluster in the Galaxy
abstract: Finding the oldest globular cluster of the Galaxy is important to constrain a lower limit on the age of the Galaxy and the Universe. VVV CL001 ([l,b]= [5.26,0.77]) is perhaps the most metal-poor ([Fe/H]~-2.2 dex) globular cluster in the Galactic bulge and a promising candidate to be the oldest globular cluster in the entire Milky Way. Due to its recent discovery and high extinction, its physical parameters, especially the distance and age, remain highly uncertain, yet they are essential to define it as an ancient native stellar system of the Milky Way. We aim to refine the distance and age of VVV CL001 using deep and high-quality photometry, to study its role in the formation of the Milky Way, and to determine whether it is the oldest Galactic globular cluster. We used J and KS observations to construct the deepest CMD of VVV CL001 to date, based on FourStar/Baade PSF photometry combined with HST near-IR wide-filter PSF photometry. We selected cluster members through proper motion calculations and the HDBSCAN algorithm, and assigned membership probabilities via Markov-Chain Monte Carlo iterations in a 5-dimensional parameter space. Using r band data from DECam/Blanco, we optically identified horizontal branch members and applied an isochrone-fitting technique to determine the cluster distance, while members around the main-sequence turn-off yielded the age from different isochrone sets. Finally, we refined the cluster orbital parameters. We obtained a distance of d = 7.34 +- 0.46 kpc, the most precise to date. We derived an age of 13.4 +- 0.4 Gyr, indicating that VVV CL001 is one of the oldest globular clusters in the Galaxy. The orbit confirms that the cluster belongs to the Galactic bulge, which, together with its age and metallicity, could link it to the early proto-Milky Way assembly, extending the metal-poor end of the known in situ globular clusters.

title: Constraining Solid HNCO and Its Environment in Open JWST Data with Laboratory Spectra
abstract: The presence of HNCO in the gaseous phase is well known for the interstellar medium, but the molecule is not detected yet in the solid phase. We report the first laboratory-confirmed identification of solid HNCO at 2260 cm$^{-1}$ in open JWST data using laboratory infrared spectra. For that, we grew binary mixtures of HNCO with main constituents of interstellar ice using ISEAge setup at 10 K: HNCO:H$_2$O = 1:10, HNCO:CO = 1:10, HNCO:CO$_2$ = 1:10, HNCO:CH$_3$OH~=~1:10. We present transmission infrared spectra of pure HNCO and HNCO-bearing ices along with the corresponding band strengths at 10 K. The fitting of open JWST observational data with the laboratory reference spectra in a 10--23 K temperature range show that solid HNCO is predominantly located in the apolar layer rich in CO. The abundance of solid HNCO is approximately estimated as 0.04--0.15\% relative to solid H$_2$O. The positive correlation between HNCO and N$_2$O suggests their co-formation via the chemical route that includes solid N$_2$. The results are also supported by the numerical modeling of HNCO formation in protostellar objects with predicted abundance of 0.06--0.11\%. We calculated the upper limits for CH$_3$CN toward two protostars and evaluated its abundance to solid water using the spectroscopic fitting and modeling.

title: Single-Parameter Exponential Model Outperforms Standard Dark Matter and Modified Newtonian Frameworks in Predicting Galactic Rotation Curves
abstract: The functional forms of galactic rotation curves provide a fundamental test for models of gravity and dark matter. In this work, we conduct a rigorous statistical comparison of five distinct models against the complete sample of 175 galaxies from the SPARC database. The models under consideration are: (1) a one-parameter empirical law, physically constrained by each galaxy's measured flat disc rotation velocity ($V_{\text{flat}}$); (2) a classical two-parameter Freeman disk; (3) a three-parameter Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) dark matter halo plus baryons model; (4) a one-parameter Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) model; and (5) a two-parameter Bosma/Dark Matter Disk model. We employ a Bayesian framework with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for parameter estimation, and use the Akaike Information Criterion (AICc) to assess the goodness-of-fit and statistical parsimony of the best-fit models. Our results reveal a decisive preference for the constrained one-parameter empirical model. It is selected as the best descriptor for a clear majority of the sample (60.6\%) and, critically, also achieves the best median goodness-of-fit, with a reduced chi-squared of $χ^2_ν = 0.41$. In contrast, the standard NFW framework is preferred in only 12.6\% of cases, while the MOND and Freeman disk models are selected as optimal for just 10.3\% and 9.1\%, respectively. The Bosma model, despite linking dynamics to the gas distribution, is preferred in only 7.4\% of cases. The pronounced statistical and descriptive success of this simple, physically-anchored law over more complex, established theories suggests that its functional form represents a fundamental and highly efficient organizing principle in the dynamics of disk galaxies.

title: The chemical evolution of the LMC from APOGEE abundances: a hybrid two-infall OMEGA+ analysis
abstract: The Large Magellanic Cloud (LMC) provides resolved stellar abundances and star-formation histories that can be used together to test models of dwarf-galaxy chemical evolution. We investigated if the non-monotonic APOGEE $[\mathrm{Mg}/\mathrm{Fe}]$-$[\mathrm{Fe}/\mathrm{H}]$ sequence can be explained by a hybrid history that combines a second gas-infall episode with a temporary increase in star-formation efficiency (SFE). We selected 4933 LMC red-giant-branch stars from APOGEE-2 DR17. We fitted an adaptively binned median Mg sequence with the two-zone open-box code OMEGA+. The formal fitting objective contained only the Mg sequence. The metallicity distribution function (MDF), one-dimensional abundance distributions, star-formation history (SFH), present-day mass partition, SFR, and supernova (SN) rate were retained as posterior diagnostics. The best-fitting model reproduces the Mg sequence with an RMS residual of 0.01 dex and also gives a close posterior match to O. It contains two delayed-tau infall episodes, with the second beginning at $t_2=10.39$ Gyr and with integrated mass ratio $M_2/M_1=0.159$, followed by a temporary Gaussian SFE enhancement centred at $t=11.91$ Gyr. The second infall is represented by a mixture of enriched and primordial gas. The model reproduces the timing of the late SFH enhancement and yields a present SFR within the adopted comparison range. A hybrid second-infall and SFE-enhancement history is a plausible scenario for reproducing the observed LMC Mg median sequence. Our fit explains the LMC evolution fairly well, but the remaining small MDF, mass, and SN-rate discrepancies suggest that a selection-function-aware treatment of the stellar distributions is required for a stricter comparison.

title: Probing the Optical/UV Continuum Variability of Active Galactic Nuclei with the Damped Random Walk Model
abstract: Optical/UV continuum variability over baselines of up to 20 yr is investigated using the damped random walk (DRW) model for 1214 active galactic nuclei (AGNs) compiled from Y. Shen et al. and C. J. Burke et al. Among these, 115 AGNs with reliable DRW fitting and unbiased DRW parameters (timescale $τ_{2500}$ and amplitude $σ_{2500}$ at the rest-frame 2500~Å) are used to examine the relations between the variability and the accretion properties. We found a significant correlation of $τ_{2500}$ with black hole mass ($M_{\rm BH}$) and dimensionless accretion rate ($\dot{\mathscr{M}}$) of the form $τ_{2500} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{0.50\pm0.07} \dot{\mathscr{M}}^{0.27\pm0.04}$, while the dependence on the continuum luminosity at 5100~Å and redshift becomes insignificant after controlling for $M_{\rm BH}$. $τ_{2500}$ also correlate with the mass accretion rate ($\dot{M}$) as $τ_{2500} \propto \dot{M}^{0.41\pm0.04}$, which is consistent with the thermal timescale expected from the standard thin-disk model within $3σ$ uncertainties; while the average value is consistent with the expectations of the model, the scatter in the relation can be due to differences in the viscosity parameter ($α$) or in disk temperature profiles. Assuming that \tauuv\ corresponds to the accretion disk thermal timescale, the disk-emitting radius at rest-frame 2500~Å ($R_{2500}$) is found to correlate with $M_{\rm BH}$ as $R_{2500} \propto M_{\rm BH}^{0.53\pm0.05}$. Using the microlensing-based $R_{2500}-M_{\rm BH}$ relation of C. W. Morgan et al., $α$ is statistically estimated to be $0.04\pm0.01$.

title: Cosmic-ray melt windows in interstellar ice make a four-carbon ketose but not the sugar pattern of G+0.693-0.027
abstract: Erythrulose (ERU), a four-carbon (C4) ketose, is reported towards the Galactic-centre cloud G+0.693-0.027 at a column density comparable to that of glycolaldehyde (GA), while the three-carbon (C3) sugars are not detected. We test whether melt windows opened in interstellar ice by cosmic-ray heavy ions can reproduce this pattern, with each rate fixed to a published value where available. A track model for eleven cosmic-ray nuclei determines the rate and duration of the liquid windows and the energy deposited inside and outside the melts. A radical network including C1 radicals from formaldehyde and methanol follows the inventory through repeated events. Radiolysis between events uses measured half-life doses of organics in cold ice. Hydrated GA opens a channel that preferentially forms the C4 ketose, so the melt-window chemistry can account for the ketose identity of ERU, although cold surface chemistry also yields it. The overall pattern, however, is not reproduced. The C1 radicals add one carbon at a time: dihydroxyacetone is at 15 times its limit when ERU/GA reaches the observed value. The ions deposit 0.41 eV per molecule per event outside the melts, which destroys the sugars between events; the ratio is reached only for half-life doses above 1000 eV, against measured values below 5 eV. The exposure is less certain: 2940 whole-grain melting events, 65 Myr at an ionisation rate $ζ=10^{-14}$ s$^{-1}$. Within 7 Myr it needs $ζ\gtrsim9.3\times10^{-14}$ s$^{-1}$, 9.3 times the dense-gas limit in the Central Molecular Zone, or $5.8\times10^{-15}$ s$^{-1}$ if the trapped radicals recombine. With standard assumptions the sugars of G+0.693 are not made in cosmic-ray melt windows. The pattern would need C1 radicals that do not add to the sugar radicals, sugars that survive the solid-phase dose and a local source of MeV ions with $ζ\gtrsim2\times10^{-13}$ s$^{-1}$.

title: A $\wedge$-like metallicity profile in the disk of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy
abstract: Unveiling the properties of the progenitors that formed the tidal structures of the Milky Way (MW) is essential for exploring the MW's assembly history. Such studies further afford a unique opportunity to dissect the formation and evolution of dwarf galaxies by contrasting surviving and disrupted systems. However, reconstructing the intrinsic structure of progenitors solely from the positions and velocities of their tidal debris remains a formidable challenge. Here, we decode the chemo-kinematic signatures embedded in the stellar streams of the Sagittarius (Sgr) dwarf galaxy through N-body simulations. Our simulation reproduces a vertical metallicity gradient in the Sgr streams. We show that this feature is naturally explained if the stream originated from a disk component with a $\wedge$-like metallicity profile. Remarkably, similar metallicity profiles are identified in MaNGA survey data for a few (3/217) field dwarf galaxies, suggesting this feature is rare but not unique to Sgr. The vertical metallicity gradient of stellar streams preserves extra detailed galactic fossil records, enabling quantitative reconstruction of the peculiar structure of the satellite galaxy. The similar metallicity profiles of Sgr and MW raise the question of a possible special coevolution.
